title: Hawaiian Airlines To Retire Boeing 717 Fleet, Shift to Larger 737s for Inter-Island Flights
excerpt: Alaska Air Group will replace Hawaiian's 19 aging Boeing 717s with 737 Next Generation jets starting in 2028, boosting inter-island seat capacity by 25% while nearly doubling its cargo freighter fleet.
body:
• Hawaiian Airlines will retire all 19 Boeing 717s, replacing them with Boeing 737 Next Generation jets beginning in 2028, increasing seat capacity from 128 to roughly 160 per aircraft.
  • Alaska Air Group is also leasing four Boeing 737-800 converted freighters, nearly doubling its cargo fleet from five to nine aircraft.
  • The moves fall under Alaska's "Accelerate" growth framework, with integrated cargo operations projected to generate $150 million in new annual profit.
  • Southwest Airlines already flies Boeing 737 MAX 8s on Hawaiian inter-island routes, providing a working model for larger jets on short-hop service.

Hawaiian Airlines will phase out its entire fleet of 19 Boeing 717s — all more than two decades old — and replace them with larger 737 Next Generation jets for inter-island service starting in 2028, parent company Alaska Air Group announced on Tuesday.

The 737 NGs seat approximately 160 passengers, a 25% increase over the 717s' 128-seat configuration. Hawaiian CEO Diana Birkett Rakow told Reuters the airline needs the additional capacity to meet growing midday demand on its short inter-island routes connecting Honolulu, Maui, Kona, and other island airports.

"The default at this point will be 737s. I think it's the most likely answer to replace the 717s."

— Shane Tackett, President, Alaska Airlines

A Fleet Built for a Different Era

Hawaiian's 717s have served as the backbone of its inter-island network since 2001, purpose-built for the 100-seat market and engineered to handle the high-cycle, short-haul operations in Hawaii's corrosive salt air. Flights between islands often last just 25 to 45 minutes, and the 717's quick-turn capabilities made it ideal for the high-frequency schedule Hawaiian maintained.

But the aircraft have grown increasingly expensive to maintain, with no direct modern successor available. Alaska Airlines President Shane Tackett, speaking at the IATA Annual General Meeting in Rio de Janeiro last month, signaled that the transition was coming, though he noted it was "not imminent" at the time, according to The Air Current.

The formal announcement now puts a concrete timeline on the shift: 2028. Alternative aircraft such as the Airbus A220 and Embraer E195-E2 had been discussed as potential replacements, but Alaska opted for fleet commonality. Running a single aircraft family across the combined airline reduces training costs, simplifies maintenance, and streamlines spare parts inventories.

Cargo Fleet Doubles Under Accelerate Plan

Alongside the passenger fleet overhaul, Alaska Air Group announced long-term leases for four Boeing 737-800 converted freighter aircraft, nearly doubling its dedicated cargo fleet from five to nine planes. The freighters are slated to enter service in 2028 and will operate between the carrier's major hubs in Seattle, Anchorage, and Honolulu.

Aircraft assigned to Hawaiian routes will carry the Hawaiian Air Cargo livery, preserving the brand's identity while operating under Alaska's unified systems. Alaska Air Cargo is the only legacy U.S. passenger carrier that maintains a dedicated freighter division, transporting more than 370 million pounds of cargo annually across over 100 airports.

Corporate leadership said the cargo expansion is a foundational element of the broader Alaska Accelerate strategic framework, projecting that integrated cargo operations will deliver $150 million in new annual profit while opening international shipping routes out of Seattle-Tacoma International Airport.

What It Means for Hawaii-Bound Travelers

For the millions of tourists who visit Hawaii each year — including a growing number of Indian-American families drawn to the islands — the transition promises tangible benefits. More seats per aircraft means better availability on popular inter-island hops like Honolulu to Kahului or Kona, particularly during peak travel seasons when the 717s often filled up fast.

Southwest Airlines already operates Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft on inter-island routes, demonstrating that larger narrowbody jets can function effectively on sectors as short as 100 miles. Alaska's move further validates this model and may intensify competition on routes where Southwest has been the only carrier offering 737-class capacity.

Shifting heavy freight to dedicated cargo planes also frees belly-hold space on passenger jets, reducing the likelihood of checked-bag bumping during busy holiday periods — a familiar frustration for travelers hauling luggage between islands.

Looking Ahead

The 717 retirement marks the end of an era for Hawaiian's domestic operations, but the carrier's broader fleet remains intact. Hawaiian continues to fly Airbus A321neos on West Coast routes and A330-200s on long-haul Pacific services, while Alaska's 787 Dreamliners handle the group's expanding transcontinental and international network from Seattle.

The key question now is execution. Transitioning 19 aircraft on a high-frequency network without disrupting service will require careful scheduling, and Alaska will need to ensure the larger 737s don't introduce excess capacity on less-trafficked routes. For now, the 717s will continue flying until the 737s are ready — giving passengers a few more years with the compact jets that have defined island-hopping in Hawaii for a quarter-century.
